# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Clinical and Evidence-Based Review

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major driver of ischemic stroke, primarily due to thrombus formation within the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. While oral anticoagulants (OAC) remain the first-line therapy for stroke prevention, their long-term use is frequently limited by bleeding complications, poor compliance, and absolute contraindications. To address these limitations, percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as a validated non-pharmacological alternative for stroke prophylaxis.

## Clinical Evidence and Evolution of Devices

The clinical development of LAAC was established by the randomized PROTECT AF [1] and PREVAIL [2] trials, which compared the first-generation Watchman device to warfarin. Long-term five-year data confirmed that Watchman offered comparable stroke prevention with a significant reduction in major bleeding, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality compared to warfarin [3]. While initially tested in patients who could tolerate short-term OAC, the ASAP study demonstrated the safety and efficacy of the Watchman device in patients with absolute contraindications to OAC, utilizing dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) post-procedure [4]. The prospective EWOLUTION registry validated these findings in a real-world, high-bleeding-risk cohort [5].

The therapeutic landscape has since expanded to compare LAAC directly with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs). The PRAGUE-17 trial, which randomized high-risk AF patients to either LAAC (mostly Watchman or Amplatzer Amulet) or DOACs, demonstrated that LAAC was non-inferior to DOACs regarding the composite endpoint of stroke, cardiovascular death, or clinically significant bleeding at both 2-year [6] and 4-year follow-ups [7].

Device design has evolved significantly to improve procedural safety and seal efficacy. The Amulet IDE trial directly compared the Amplatzer Amulet (a disc-and-lobe occluder) with the first-generation Watchman, proving non-inferiority for stroke prevention and showing a higher rate of complete appendage closure [8]. Meanwhile, the next-generation Watchman FLX device, which features a fully closed end and more anchors to minimize leaks, showed excellent procedural safety and low complication rates in the PINNACLE FLX trial [9]. The SWISS-APERO trial, a direct head-to-head randomized trial comparing Amulet with Watchman FLX, revealed similar clinical efficacy, although Amulet had a slightly higher rate of complete closure at the expense of more peri-procedural complications [10]. Real-world registries, such as the global Amulet observational study [11] and assessments of the Chinese-developed LAmbre device [12], continue to document high implant success rates across varied anatomies. Concurrently, surgical exclusion of the LAA, evaluated in the LAAOS III trial, has reaffirmed the critical role of LAA management in stroke reduction during concomitant cardiac surgery [13].

## Procedural Technique, Imaging, and Patient Selection

Anatomical variation of the LAA (e.g., chicken wing, windswept, broccoli, cactus) heavily influences device selection and procedural success [14]. According to the EHRA/EAPCI consensus statement, patient selection should focus on those with high stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc score) and high bleeding risk (HAS-BLED score) or those who experience thromboembolic events despite therapeutic anticoagulation [15]. Large national registries, such as the NCDR LAAO registry, underscore that procedural success has significantly improved over the last decade, with a corresponding drop in major adverse events [16,17].

A successful LAAC procedure depends on meticulous transseptal puncture, which is ideally performed in the inferoposterior quadrant of the fossa ovalis to facilitate optimal device alignment [18]. Multimodality imaging is central to this process. Pre-procedural cardiac computed tomography (CT) allows for accurate three-dimensional sizing and anatomical characterization [19]. Intraprocedurally, transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) remains the standard of care, but intracardiac echocardiography (ICE) has emerged as a reliable alternative that avoids general anesthesia and minimizes esophageal trauma [20].

## Complications and Post-Procedural Management

Despite technological advances, LAAC is associated with specific complications, notably device-related thrombus (DRT) and peridevice leak (PDL). DRT occurs in 2% to 4% of patients and is associated with an increased risk of stroke [21,22]. Management typically involves restarting OAC until thrombus resolution is confirmed on imaging. Residual PDLs, particularly those greater than 5 mm, have historically been considered clinically significant; however, recent data suggest that even smaller leaks (e.g., >2 mm) are associated with a higher long-term risk of thromboembolic events [23].

Post-procedural antithrombotic regimens vary based on the implanted device and patient bleeding risk [24]. The classical regimen for the Watchman device consists of 45 days of OAC followed by DAPT up to 6 months, and aspirin monotherapy thereafter, whereas the Amulet is often managed with DAPT from the outset. For patients completely unable to tolerate OAC, the ASAP-TOO trial design sought to evaluate LAAC versus single antiplatelet therapy or no therapy, though it was terminated early due to slow enrollment [25].

## Economic Value and Future Directions

LAAC has proven to be highly cost-effective, offering cost-utility over both warfarin and DOACs within several years post-implantation due to the front-loaded costs being offset by long-term reductions in bleeding and stroke hospitalizations [26]. Its application is also being explored in highly complex populations, such as end-stage renal disease patients on dialysis, who represent an ultra-high-risk cohort [27].

The field continues to evolve rapidly with several ongoing, large-scale randomized trials. The OPTION trial is evaluating Watchman FLX against OAC in patients undergoing catheter ablation for AF [28], while the CATALYST trial is comparing the Amplatzer Amulet directly against DOAC therapy [29]. These investigations, along with novel device designs and refined imaging protocols, will further define the role of LAAC in the modern cardiovascular therapeutic landscape [30].
